photo.caption: An early Western Han dynasty (202 BC – 9 AD) silk map found in tomb 3 of Mawangdui Han tombs site, depicting the Kingdom of Changsha and Kingdom of Nanyue in southern China (note: the south direction is oriented at the top, north at the bottom).
photo.description: A Chinese topographic map (with the south positioned at the top) from Mawangdui tomb 3; dated to the early Western Han period (183–168 BC); length is 96 cm; width is 96 cm; the map is made of ink on silk. It is now housed in the Hunan Provincial Museum, Changsha. The map depicts a large territory in southern China spanning from the imperial fiefdom of Changsha (a semi-autonomous kingdom within the Han Empire, now modern-day Hunan) to the independent and sometimes hostile Kingdom of Nanyue in what is now modern-day Guangdong and northern Vietnam

photo.caption: The Yu Ji Tu, or Map of the Tracks of Yu Gong, carved into stone in 1137, located in the Stele Forest of Xi'an. This 3 ft (0.91 m) squared map features a graduated scale of 100 li for each rectangular grid. China's coastline and river systems are clearly defined and precisely pinpointed on the map. Yu Gong is in reference to the Chinese deity described in the geographical chapter of the Classic of History, dated 5th century BC.
photo.description: The Chinese Yu Ji Tu (Map of the Tracks of Yu the Great), a map carved into stone in the year 1137 during the Song Dynasty, located in the Stele Forest of modern-day Xian, China. Yu the Great refers to the Chinese deity described in the Chinese geographical work of the Yu Gong, a chapter of the Classic of History. Needham and Chavannes assert that the original map must have predated the 12th century. photo.description: A seminal map. This is the first Japanese printed map to depict the world, including Europe and America, from a Buddhist cosmographical perspective. Printed by woodblock in 1710 (Hoei 7), this map was composed by the Buddhist monk Rokashi Hotan. Inspired by the 1653 publication of the Xiyouji (西游记, Jap. photo.description: Copy of Al Idrisi Tabula Rogeriana with arabic names transliterated into the roman alphabet. The original has north at the bottom, so it appears "upside down". Please do not rotate it to have north at the top, as we seek to preserve the original.

photo.caption: Surviving fragment of the first World Map of Piri Reis (1513) showing parts of the Americas.
photo.description: Map of the world by Ottoman admiral Piri Reis, drawn in 1513. Only part of the original map survives and is held at the Topkapi Museum in Istanbul. The map synthesizes information from many maps, including one drawn by Christopher Columbus of the Caribbean.
photo.section: Piri Reis map of the Ottoman Empire

photo.caption: The Gough Map, a road map of 14th-century Britain
photo.description: The Gough Map or Bodleian Map is a road map of Great Britain, dating from around 1360. The Gough Map is the oldest extant map of the roads of medieval Britain. It is about 115 x 56cm large and was made around 1360. It is named after Richard Gough, who donated the map to the Bodleian Library in 1809. East is on the top.

Now held by the Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana in Florence, Italy.
photo.section: Padrón Real of the Spanish Empire

photo.caption: The Propaganda Map, a 1529 version of the Padrón Real now held by the Vatican Library.
photo.description: c. 1887 reproduction on two sheets of the 1529 Propaganda world map, believed to be a reproduction by Diogo Ribeiro of the Spanish Padron Real (Royal Standard Map) held at the Seville Casa de Contratacion (House of Trade). It shows Spanish uncertainty regarding the Pacific Coast of the Americas, the Spice Islands, and the exact details of locations around the Indian Ocean, while adding additional information from the expeditions of Magellan and others. See here for further history and background.
photo.section: Padrón Real of the Spanish Empire

pages.text: Maps help humans find their way. When people first made maps is unclear. Ancient cultures like Babylon, Greece, Rome, China, and India made them. Early maps did not show Earth as round. People did not know the true shape of the Earth.

Finding the very first map is hard. Some ancient artifacts might be maps, but experts are not sure. A clay tablet from ancient Babylonia shows a river valley. Scholars date this small tablet to the twenty-fourth century BC.

In China, old maps also survived. Workers found ancient Chinese maps drawn on wooden blocks. These maps date back to the fourth century BC. Other silk maps were found in ancient tombs from the second century BC.

Ancient Greek scholars studied the world too. A Greek scholar named Eratosthenes calculated the size of the Earth. He used lines on his maps to find places. Another scholar named Ptolemy used math to make better maps.

Today, making maps is much easier. Airplanes and satellites take pictures of the land. Free online services let people see accurate maps of the whole world. Maps are now more accessible than ever before.

B1-B2.headline: How Humans Learned to Map the World

pages.text: Maps have long allowed humans to explain and navigate the world. Although the exact origin remains unclear, early maps were independently invented by many cultures. Ancient civilizations such as Babylon, Greece, Rome, China, and India produced maps extensively.

Early mapmakers ignored the curvature of the Earth. This happened partly because the true shape was unknown and partly because small areas do not need curve corrections. However, maps of larger regions eventually used projections from model globes to control distortion.

Identifying the oldest surviving map is difficult because ancient definitions and artifacts are not always precise. In Babylonia, surveyors created accurate maps on clay tablets. For instance, a small tablet from Ga-Sur shows a river valley between hills.

In China, wooden block maps from the fourth century BC survived because they stayed soaked in underground water. Later excavations found silk maps from the Han dynasty. Ancient Chinese writers also recorded geographical descriptions in early texts.

Hellenistic Greek scholars introduced major scientific changes. Eratosthenes calculated the Earth's circumference and used a grid of lines to reference locations. Later, Ptolemy used astronomy and mathematics to improve map projections and coordinate systems.

Maps in Ancient Babylonia were made by using accurate surveying techniques. For example, a clay tablet found at Ga-Sur shows a river valley between two hills. Cuneiform inscriptions label the features on the map, including a plot of land owned by Azala. Hills are shown by overlapping semicircles, rivers by lines, and cities by circles.

Maps represent a fundamental human invention designed for navigation and spatial explanation. While the precise inception of cartography remains obscure, rudimentary local maps emerged independently across diverse societies, including ancient Babylon, Greece, Rome, China, and India.

Early cartographers initially disregarded planetary curvature, reflecting both prevailing ignorance of Earth's true geometry and the negligible distortion over limited extents. Following Classical Greece, regional and global cartography increasingly relied on model projections to manage inevitable geometric distortion.

Establishing a definitive earliest map is problematic due to ambiguous artifact classifications. Nevertheless, surviving archeological evidence demonstrates advanced Babylonian surveying, exemplified by a clay tablet depicting a river valley with cuneiform topographical labels.

Chinese cartographic heritage includes fourth-century BC wooden block maps preserved via water-logged subterranean conditions, alongside subsequent Han dynasty silk maps. Concurrently, early Chinese texts documented provincial economic, geographic, and agricultural systems.

Hellenistic scholarship introduced mathematical rigor to geography. Eratosthenes computed the terrestrial circumference and pioneered coordinate charting using meridians and parallels. Subsequently, Ptolemy refined perspective projection and coordinate systems to enhance mapping precision.

Contemporary cartography benefits from advanced transport, surveillance aviation, and satellite imagery, enabling the documentation of remote terrains. Digital platforms now provide unprecedented global access to precise cartographic data.
